items.title: Push attribution for commits in limited public preview
items.author: Allison
items.excerpt: GitHub now durably records the authenticated user who pushed each commit and surfaces that pusher identity in the UI and API alongside the existing author and committer fields. Commit author and committer fields are just strings that the pushing client supplies, so anyone with write access to a repository can set them to any name and email they choose. That makes it possible for an attacker who compromises a low-privilege account to forge commits that appear to come from a trusted maintainer, evading review policies and confusing audit trails. GitHub already authenticates pushes. This release adds durable, per-commit pusher attribution alongside the author and committer metadata. With this release: Every commit pushed to a repository now has a durable, authenticated pusher identity attached to it, independent of whatever the author and committer metadata claims. A new repository rule condition, Committer must match pusher, blocks pushes where the committer metadata doesn’t match any verified email address of the authenticated pusher. This closes a path for commit identity spoofing. You can use the pusher identity to spot-check suspicious activity or speed up security investigations instead of relying on unverified metadata. You can do this because the pusher identity is now visible wherever commits are shown instead. To enforce stricter identity requirements on a repository, add the new Committer must match pusher rule to a ruleset. Push attribution is available now as a limited public preview for GitHub Enterprise customers. If you are interested in joining the preview, please contact your account team and request access. Learn more about configuring push rulesets. The post Push attribution for commits in limited public preview appeared first on The GitHub Blog.
items.why_it_matters: GitHub now records who actually pushed each commit, which helps catch forged commit authors in supply-chain attacks. It is relevant to audit trails and review policies on our and client repos.

items.title: Hello Python 3.15, goodbye 3.10, and now I can use 3.11
items.excerpt: Python 3.15 is here! Here's the essential What's new in Python 3.15 guide, this year curated by 3.14 and 3.15 release manager Hugo van Kemenade. As someone who builds open source software that works in every supported Python version, I get to say goodbye to Python 3.10 and start embracing features from Python 3.11. First, some highlights from Python 3.15. Explicit lazy imports I'm most excited about Explicit lazy imports from PEP 810. These let you import modules like so: lazy import json lazy from pathlib import Path The module will then be imported the first time those symbols are used in the code that follows. My LLM CLI tool implements plugins. I had to recommend manual lazy imports in the plugin author documentation, because simply installing plugins that used heavy dependencies such as sentence_transformers could add multiple seconds to every invocation of the llm command. Lazy imports directly address this startup cost. Unpacking in comprehensions The new [*sublist for sublist in lists] unpacking syntax is neat. Here's an illustration lifted from the documentation: lists = [[1, 2], [3, 4], [5]] [*L for L in lists] # [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] # equivalent to [x for L in lists for x in L] sets = [{1, 2}, {2, 3}, {3, 4}] {*s for s in sets} # {1, 2, 3, 4} # equivalent to {x for s in sets for x in s} dicts = [{'a': 1}, {'b': 2}, {'a': 3}] {**d for d in dicts} # {'a': 3, 'b': 2} # equivalent to {k: v for d in dicts for k,v in d.items()} PEP 798: Unpacking in Comprehensions by Adam Hartz and Erik Demaine proposed this as an extension of the unpacking syntax from PEP 448, which landed in Python 3.5 back in 2015. A sampling profiler Python's existing tracing profiler has been renamed from cProfile to profiling.tracing, and has been joined by an exciting new sampling profiler called Tachyon, aka profiling.sampling. Sampling profilers work by periodically capturing stack traces from running processes, then using those to calculate which functions have the most time spent inside o
items.why_it_matters: Python 3.15 ships with explicit lazy imports and Python 3.10 reaches end of life. Our ML work in Python should plan version upgrades and dependency support.

items.title: How Anthropic’s Dynamic Workflows Coordinate Claude Agents
items.author: Richard MacManus
items.excerpt: CJ Avilla and Harrison Stall, Members of Technical Staff at Anthropic, at AI Engineer NYC today.The AI Engineer New York 2026 conference kicked off this morning with a series of workshops, including Anthropic discussing how to orchestrate its Claude Managed Agents. Of particular interest was a brand new feature, announced on Friday, called dynamic workflows — or simply “flows,” as the presenters repeatedly called it.Flows are defined as “a new type of multiagent orchestration, built for your most ambitious workloads.”CJ Avilla and Harrison Stall, both Members of Technical Staff at Anthropic, began by invoking some operating system projects of the past — from Ken Thompson building the original Unix operating system, through to Linux evolving from one person (Linus Torvalds) to layers of trusted maintainers. items.title: Pi Durable PROACTIVE Agents: Jev Triggers My ON-CALL Pi Agent
items.author: IndyDevDan
items.excerpt: Engineers... your agents are LAZY. 😲 They sit in a terminal and wait for YOU to prompt them. The future belongs to PROACTIVE agents: durable agents that don't wait for you to work. A durable Pi agent persists your ongoing work, conversations, and application state through failures, through clients, and through change itself. I have durable agents running right now on my M4 Mac Mini, my M6 Mac Mini, my M5 MacBook Pro, and exe.dev cloud sandboxes, all connected in one durable agent network. 🔥 Watch as a JEV classifier detects a production incident in a live log stream and triggers an ON CALL Pi agent. The agent detects, investigates, finds the root cause, writes the fix, and waits for my review. Human near the loop: I approve, it deploys, production stabilizes. JEV classified hundreds of events for pennies. items.title: Is Learning to Build Software Still Worth It with AI? (My Honest Take)
items.author: Cole Medin
items.excerpt: REA (Reverse Engineer Anything) hit #1 on GitHub Trending last week. Point your AI coding agent at an app and it works out how a feature is built, down to the binary, then rebuilds it. When AI can do THAT, is anything still worth learning? The simple answer is yes, because no model can read your mind. In this video I break down why reverse engineering works so well (the finished app already holds the intent) and the "meat proxy" trap of dumping a ticket into your coding agent and pasting back whatever comes out. Then I give you the test I use for every skill: if the next model is twice as good, does this matter more or less? ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ - Check out Firecrawl and their new tool Alexandria, the knowledge library for superintelligence: https://firecrawl.link/cole ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ - Join Dynamous for the new Agentic Coding Course 2.0 - the core of the course is now COMPLETE: https://dynamous.ai - REA GitHub (Reverse Engineer Anything): https://github.com/morluto/rea - Don't be a meat proxy (Niklas Gruhn): https://gruhn.me/blog/2026-08-03/ ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ 0:00 Reverse Engineer Anything Is Going Viral 1:26 AI Can't Read Your Mind 2:40 Don't Be a Meat Proxy 3:52 Why Reverse Engineering Works So Well 5:17 You Have to Build the Reference 6:56 Sponsor: Firecrawl 8:19 My Software Factory Example 10:22 Giving the Agent a 3D Reference 12:36 The 2x Test 12:59 What Matters Less 13:45 What Matters More 14:36 Engineers of the Harness 15:27 Final Thoughts ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ Join me as I push the limits of what is possible with AI.
